Monday: Before the spelling test, Mehak curled up on the sofa, holding her tummy. Her mother, Sonali, sat beside her, rubbed her back and gave her a small fennel sweet from the kitchen tin. "This will help settle it, sweetheart." Mehak sucked it slowly. Soon she was hunting for her pencil box.
Wednesday: The ache came again at bedtime. "Can I have the magic sweet?" Mummy gave her one and stayed until she fell asleep.
Saturday: Mummy told Papa quietly, "If these tummy aches keep coming, we'll take her to the doctor, just to check." Mehak, listening from the doorway, touched the sweet tin and felt her tummy loosen.

qa.q: What did Sonali give Mehak on Monday?
qa.a: A small fennel sweet from the kitchen tin.

qa.q: Why do you think Mehak's tummy felt better after the sweet?
qa.a: Her mother's back rub and the promise that it would help made her feel cared for and expect relief, and that calm changed how the ache felt.

qa.q: What choice did Mummy make on Saturday, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She planned to take Mehak to the doctor if the aches keep coming, so the comforting sweet helps in the moment without replacing a proper check.

qa.q: What might it be like for Mummy to see the ache come back on Wednesday?
qa.a: She may be glad the sweet and her company still calm Mehak, but also a little worried, which is why she later talks to Papa about the doctor.

grounding: A child's stomach ache eases after her caring mother gives a harmless sweet with reassurance, while the mother still plans a doctor check if it continues.

passage: Jaya, come, sit on the cot. You asked why your Uma Paati keeps jaggery in this brass box. When I was nine, in our Madurai house, I got tummy aches whenever Appa travelled for work. One night I lay crying, and he sat by me, still in his office shirt, and broke off a piece of jaggery. "Uma, this is special. Eat it slowly and the pain will go." I chewed it with my eyes shut while he hummed an old film song. The ache melted away, I promise you. Years later I learned it was ordinary kitchen jaggery. But his voice and his hand on my head were real medicine too. And when an ache didn't go away, he always took me to the doctor. Remember that part.

qa.q: What did Uma's Appa break off for her?
qa.a: A piece of jaggery.

qa.q: Why do you think young Uma felt the ache melt away?
qa.a: Appa told her it was special and would help, and he sat humming with his hand on her head. Feeling safe and expecting relief changed how the pain felt. 🤍

qa.q: What balance did Appa strike that a parent today could copy?
qa.a: He comforted Uma with care and a calm promise, but when an ache didn't go away, he took her to the doctor instead of relying on the jaggery.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Appa, still in his office shirt, beside his crying daughter?
qa.a: He was probably tired after work, yet he stayed and hummed to her; he may have been worried and wanted to give her something that felt like help right away.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, as a girl, her father's reassurance and a plain piece of jaggery genuinely eased her tummy ache.

passage: The night bus to Nashik was stuck in a traffic jam, rain hammering the windows, when Kunal doubled over. "Papa, my stomach hurts." Samir had no medicine and there was no shop outside, only a roll of peppermints in his jacket. He unwrapped one, pressed it into Kunal's hand and said in a calm, sure voice, "Suck this slowly. It helps tummies on long journeys. Put your head here." Kunal leaned on his shoulder. Samir rubbed small circles on his back and told him about the time a bus got stuck behind a herd of goats. By the time the traffic moved, Kunal was laughing, the ache almost gone. "If it comes back, we'll see a doctor in Nashik," Samir said, and Kunal nodded, already sleepy.

qa.q: What did Samir have in his jacket?
qa.a: Only a roll of peppermints.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling by the time the traffic moved, and why?
qa.a: He felt comforted enough to laugh, because his father's calm voice, the peppermint and the goat story made him expect the ache to ease, and it did.

qa.q: With no medicine and no shops, which choices helped Samir comfort Kunal?
qa.a: He stayed calm and sure, gave the peppermint, let Kunal rest on his shoulder and told a funny story, and planned to see a doctor in Nashik if the ache came back.

qa.q: What might Samir have been feeling inside while he spoke so calmly?
qa.a: He may have been worried, stuck in the rain with no medicine, but he kept his voice steady because his calm would help Kunal feel safe.

grounding: On a stuck night bus, a boy's stomach ache eases after his father gives a harmless peppermint with calm reassurance.

passage: On the morning of the school annual day, Sunaina sat on the edge of the bed in their Hyderabad flat, holding her tummy. She was one of the six dancers in the front row. 'Mummy, it hurts. I can't go.' Nandini put down the hair clips and sat beside her. She felt Sunaina's forehead, cool. Then she went to the kitchen and came back with one small crystal of misri in her palm. 'This will help your tummy settle. Suck it slowly while I do your plait.' Nandini's voice was calm, her hands warm on Sunaina's shoulders. Sunaina sucked the sweet and watched the mirror. By the time the second plait was done, she was humming her dance song. 'Better?' 'A bit,' Sunaina said, then, 'Actually, a lot.' 'If it comes back and stays, tell me, and we'll see the doctor,' Nandini said.

'Come here, Nitin. Where?'
'Here. It's twisting.'
'Too much birthday cake at Chiku's?'
'Only two pieces. And the chips.'
'Hm.' Varun felt his forehead. 'No fever. Lie on the sofa. I have something special.'
'Medicine?'
'Better. The lemon drop from my secret tin. Every time I had a tummy ache, my mother gave me one.'
'Does it work?'
'Suck it slowly and see. I'll rub your back.'

'Good sour.'
A few minutes went by. The TV murmured.
'Papa?'
'Hm?'
'It's getting smaller. The twist.'
'Told you. Special tin.'
'Can I have another one tomorrow?'
'Only if your stomach asks nicely. And if it keeps hurting or worries you, we'll show the doctor.'

When I was eight, I got a tummy ache the night before my cousin Trisha's birthday party. I curled up on the bed and cried that I wouldn't be able to go.
Ammi sat next to me and rubbed my back. Then she took a small round sweet from the steel jar, the fennel one. "Zainab, this is a special tummy sweet. Chew it slowly. It will help."
I chewed it very slowly. She kept rubbing my back and humming. After a while, the ache got smaller and smaller. I fell asleep.
Now I know it was just a sweet. But it really did feel better. Ammi said if it had kept hurting, she would have taken me to the doctor, and I believe her.

qa.a: Ammi was probably relieved and tender, glad the ache had eased before the birthday party.

grounding: A child's stomach ache eases after a caring mother gives a harmless sweet and says it will help.

Note on the fridge for Mumma, from Joseph (Papa), Tuesday.
Arohi woke at six with a stomach ache, holding her tummy and saying the school trip would be ruined. No fever, no vomiting, she'd eaten normally last night.
I sat with her and said, "I know it hurts. Let's try Papa's trip-day mint." I gave her one of the plain mints from the tin and told her it usually helps tummies settle. She sucked it slowly while I rubbed her back and we talked about the zoo.
Within twenty minutes she was laughing and eating toast. She went on the trip.
I asked her class teacher to call if it came back. If it keeps coming on trip days, let's talk to her and see the doctor together.

qa.a: He gave her one of the plain mints from the tin.

qa.q: What was Arohi feeling when she woke at six?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worried, holding her tummy and afraid the school trip would be ruined.

qa.q: Which parts of Papa's response show good care beyond the mint?
qa.a: He sat with her, rubbed her back, talked about the zoo, asked the teacher to call if the ache returned and planned a doctor visit if it keeps happening.

qa.q: How might Mumma feel reading the note?
qa.a: Mumma may feel reassured that Arohi was cared for calmly, and thoughtful about whether trip days bring on the ache.

grounding: A child's stomach ache eases after her father gives a harmless mint with reassurance, showing expectation can change how a symptom feels.

Diary, Saturday
My stomach hurt all afternoon. I didn't want to play cricket and I lay on Dadu's cot on the terrace.
Jeevan Dadu came up with a small paper twist. Inside were two lumps of mishri. "This is my old trick," he said. "Mishri and a little rest, and the ache goes. It always worked for your papa."
I held it on my tongue while he told me about the monkey that stole his lunch in 1972. I laughed so much I forgot about my stomach. When I remembered, it was mostly gone.
Dadu said, "If it comes back tomorrow, we'll show the doctor." It didn't come back.
Maybe it was the mishri. Maybe it was the monkey.
Anirban

qa.q: What was inside the paper twist?
qa.a: Inside were two lumps of mishri.

qa.q: Why did Anirban's stomach ache seem to fade?
qa.a: Anirban felt comforted and amused by Dadu's reassurance and the monkey story, so expecting the mishri to help made the ache feel smaller.

qa.q: What part of Jeevan Dadu's response was wise?
qa.a: Along with the mishri and story, he promised to show the doctor if the ache came back, so comfort didn't replace proper care.

qa.q: How might Jeevan Dadu have felt when Anirban laughed?
qa.a: Dadu probably felt warm and pleased, happy that his old trick and his story cheered Anirban up.

grounding: A child's stomach ache eases after a grandfather gives harmless mishri and reassurance, showing how expectation changes a symptom.

Sabina, you have a tummy ache? Come, let your Nani Deepika tell you a winter story.
When I was nine, in Lucknow, I often got stomach aches in the cold months. My Ammi would sit by my quilt and give me one small lump of mishri. "This will make it better," she'd say, and stroke my hair.
And it did! Within a little while, I'd feel lighter. I thought mishri was medicine.
Years later, I asked her. She laughed. "It was just sugar. It was me sitting with you that helped." But she also said, "If it didn't go away, I always took you to the doctor." And she did, twice.

qa.q: How did Deepika's Ammi see the mishri?

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a child whose stomach ache eased after a caring mother gave sugar and reassurance, while lasting pain still went to the doctor.
